recordings.title: Opening · Listen
recordings.text:
Why can siblings with the same parents look so different? A chromosome shuffle!

Most of your body’s cells have two chromosome sets: one from mom and one from dad. Matching chromosomes form homologous pairs. They carry the same genes in the same places, but may have different versions, called alleles.

In cells that make eggs or sperm, DNA is copied once, then the cell divides twice. The first division separates homologous chromosomes. The second separates sister chromatids. That leaves haploid products with one chromosome set. In humans, that’s twenty-three chromosomes instead of forty-six. Mixing DNA and halving the sets? That’s meiosis! Swipe through the eight steps with me!

recordings.title: Prophase I
recordings.text:
First up is prophase one: time to pair up and trade a little DNA.

Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Homologous chromosomes are matching partners, one from each parent. They carry the same genes in the same positions, but their alleles can differ. Synapsis: Homologous chromosomes pair, forming tetrads (four chromatids). Crossing over: Non-sister chromatids exchange matching DNA segments at chiasmata (crossover points). Genetic variation: New allele combinations are created. Nuclear envelope breaks down, centrosomes move apart, and the spindle forms.

recordings.title: Metaphase I
recordings.text:
In metaphase one, the pairs get ready for their big lineup.

Homologous chromosome pairs (tetrads) align at the cell equator. Spindle fibers attach to kinetochores on homologous chromosomes. Each pair orients independently, called independent assortment, creating genetic variation.

recordings.title: Anaphase I
recordings.text:
Anaphase one sends the homologs on separate journeys.

Spindle fibers pull homologous chromosomes to opposite poles. Sister chromatids remain joined at their centromeres. Homologs separate, reducing the chromosome sets by half.

recordings.title: Telophase I
recordings.text:
Telophase one wraps up the first division.

Homologous chromosomes reach opposite poles; nuclear envelopes may re-form. Cytokinesis divides the cell into two haploid cells. Each cell has 23 replicated chromosomes (46 chromatids). Haploid means one set of chromosomes.

recordings.title: Prophase II
recordings.text:
Welcome to prophase two: another division, without another round of copying.

Spindles form in both haploid cells. Chromosomes re-condense if needed, and nuclear envelopes break down. No DNA replication occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II.

recordings.title: Metaphase II
recordings.text:
In metaphase two, it’s single file in both cells.

Chromosomes align single-file at the cell equator. Spindle fibers attach to sister kinetochores from opposite poles. Each cell has 23 chromosomes, each containing two sister chromatids.

recordings.title: Anaphase II
recordings.text:
Anaphase two is the sisters’ big send-off.

Centromeres divide, and sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles. Each separated chromatid is now an individual chromosome. Crossing over may make sister chromatids genetically different.

recordings.title: Telophase II
recordings.text:
Finally, telophase two brings the chromosome shuffle home.

Nuclear envelopes re-form, and chromosomes uncoil. Cytokinesis produces four haploid cells, each with 23 single-chromatid chromosomes. In egg formation (oogenesis), unequal cytokinesis produces one large egg and small polar bodies.

recordings.title: Copy once · Divide twice
recordings.text: Let’s follow the chromosomes in a human example. Before meiosis, one diploid cell has forty-six chromosomes in twenty-three pairs. After DNA is copied, it still has forty-six chromosomes, but now there are ninety-two chromatids. Meiosis one separates homologs. Each of the two cells has twenty-three chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids. There’s no extra round of DNA copying. Meiosis two separates the sisters. Each of the four haploid products has twenty-three single-chromatid chromosomes. In egg formation, the cytoplasm divides unequally, giving one large egg and small polar bodies. The four products do not become four functional eggs.

recordings.title: Meet the key players
recordings.text: Meet the chromosome shuffling crew! Pick a player to hear its description, or explore crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilization. Each recording starts when you tap its speaker.

recordings.title: Meiosis I vs. meiosis II
recordings.text: Meiosis I vs. meiosis II. Meiosis I is reduction division: homologous chromosomes separate, reducing two chromosome sets to one. Meiosis II is equational division: sister chromatids separate while each final product retains one chromosome set.

recordings.title: Diploid · 2n
recordings.text: Diploid · 2n. Two chromosome sets, one inherited from each biological parent. In humans, 2n = 46 chromosomes, arranged as 23 pairs.

recordings.title: Haploid · n
recordings.text: Haploid · n. One chromosome set. Human gametes have n = 23 chromosomes. A cell can be haploid while its chromosomes still have two chromatids, as after meiosis I.

recordings.title: Somatic vs. germ cells
recordings.text: Somatic vs. germ cells. Somatic cells are body cells; mitosis supports growth and repair. Germ-line cells give rise to gametes. In animals, specialized diploid precursors in ovaries or testes enter meiosis; not every germ-line cell is always undergoing meiosis.

recordings.title: Homologous chromosomes
recordings.text:
Homologous chromosomes. Most of your body’s cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. One set of 23 came from your mom’s egg, and the other set came from your dad’s sperm. A set is the whole collection; a pair contains two matching chromosomes of one type.

Matching partners are called homologous chromosomes, or homologs. They carry the same genes in the same order and at the same positions. Each gene’s position is called its locus. Think of two editions of a recipe book: the same recipe is on the same page, but some instructions can differ.

For example, both copies of chromosome 9 carry the ABO blood-group gene at the same position. You might inherit the A allele from mom and the B allele from dad. These are different versions of the same gene. Together, these alleles usually give AB blood type.

A gene is a DNA instruction. An allele is a version of that instruction. A trait is a feature, such as your blood type, that genes help shape. Your two alleles can also be the same. Different alleles do not always change a trait.

Meiosis I separates homologous partners, so each new cell receives one chromosome from each pair. Eggs and sperm have one chromosome set rather than pairs. Human X and Y are a special case: they share only some matching regions.

recordings.title: Allele
recordings.text: Allele. An allele is a version of a gene’s DNA instructions. At the ABO gene on chromosome 9, A, B, and O are examples of alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent. For example, the A allele from mom and the B allele from dad usually give AB blood type. A and B are the alleles; blood type is the trait. Your two alleles can also match.

recordings.title: Sister chromatids
recordings.text: Sister chromatids. The two copies of a replicated chromosome, initially identical and joined at a centromere. Crossing over can make sister chromatids genetically different.

recordings.title: Centromere & kinetochore
recordings.text: Centromere & kinetochore. The centromere is the chromosome region where sisters are joined. A kinetochore is a protein complex assembled there that binds spindle microtubules.

recordings.title: Spindle fibers & centrosomes
recordings.text: Spindle fibers & centrosomes. Spindle fibers are microtubules that move chromosomes through kinetochore attachments. Centrosomes organize the animal-cell spindle and move toward opposite poles.

recordings.title: Synapsis & tetrad
recordings.text: Synapsis & tetrad. Synapsis is the close alignment of homologs during prophase I. Two replicated homologs together contain four chromatids, called a tetrad.

recordings.title: Chiasma · plural chiasmata
recordings.text: Chiasma · plural chiasmata. A visible connection between homologs at a crossover site involving non-sister chromatids.

recordings.title: Recombinant vs. parental
recordings.text: Recombinant vs. parental. Recombinant chromatids contain new mixtures of parental alleles following crossing over. Parental chromatids retain their original allele arrangement.

recordings.title: Independent assortment
recordings.text: Independent assortment. Each homologous pair orients independently at metaphase I, creating different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in meiotic products.

recordings.title: Interkinesis
recordings.text: Interkinesis. An interval between meiosis I and II in many species. No DNA replication occurs.

recordings.title: Cytokinesis
recordings.text: Cytokinesis. Division of the cytoplasm. In animal cells, a contractile ring produces a cleavage furrow. Nuclear division and cytoplasm division are distinct processes.

recordings.title: Karyotype
recordings.text: Karyotype. An ordered display of chromosomes grouped by size and other features. A typical human diploid karyotype shows 22 autosome pairs and one sex-chromosome pair, commonly XX or XY—not always XY.

recordings.title: Gamete & fertilization
recordings.text: Gamete & fertilization. A gamete is a haploid reproductive cell, such as an egg or sperm. Fertilization combines two gametes to form a diploid zygote. It occurs after meiosis.

recordings.title: Crossing over
recordings.text:
Crossing over. In prophase I, homologs align gene by gene (synapsis). Corresponding DNA segments are exchanged between non-sister chromatids. Chiasmata are the visible crossover connections.

One crossover involves two of the four chromatids: two recombinant chromatids and two unchanged parental chromatids in this example.

Sisters start as identical copies. After crossing over, they can carry different allele combinations. A crossover does not guarantee that all four products are genetically distinct in every possible case.

recordings.title: Independent assortment
recordings.text:
Independent assortment. Each homologous pair faces the poles independently at metaphase I. A maternal homolog of one pair can travel with a paternal homolog of another.

2ⁿ combinations · n = chromosome pairs
Humans: 2²³ = 8,388,608

That is the number of possible maternal/paternal chromosome combinations across many meioses, before counting crossing over—not millions of products from one division.

recordings.title: Random fertilization
recordings.text:
Random fertilization. Fertilization happens after meiosis. Any one egg can combine with any one sperm, restoring the diploid chromosome number.

8,388,608 × 8,388,608
= 70,368,744,177,664 combinations

Over 70 trillion possible chromosome combinations for a couple—even before adding crossing over.

recordings.title: Prophase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Tap each DNA bundle to pack it.

recordings.title: Prophase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Open the nuclear envelope.

recordings.title: Prophase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Drag matching homologs together—or tap to pair.

recordings.title: Prophase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Tap each chiasma to swap matching DNA segments.

recordings.title: Prophase I complete!
recordings.text:
Synapsis pairs maternal and paternal homologs gene by gene. Homologs have corresponding genes at corresponding positions and matching overall size, centromere position and banding; their alleles can differ.

Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids at chiasmata. Recombinant chromatids have new allele combinations; chromatids not involved remain parental.

recordings.title: Metaphase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Orient pairs. Choose a pole; connect its homologs.

recordings.title: Metaphase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Drag pairs to the equator—or tap to align.

recordings.title: Metaphase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Inspect the double-file lineup.

recordings.title: Metaphase I complete!
recordings.text:
Homologous pairs align double-file at the cell equator. Each replicated homolog faces an opposite pole from its partner.

In meiosis I, the sister kinetochores of one homolog connect toward the same pole. Its homolog connects toward the other pole. Sisters remain joined.

For humans, 2²³ = 8,388,608 chromosome combinations per gamete from independent assortment alone. Crossing over adds further diversity. Two illustrated pairs give 2² = 4 orientations.

recordings.title: Anaphase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Keep sisters joined at their centromeres.

recordings.title: Anaphase I · Instruction
recordings.text: Pull homologs to opposite poles.

recordings.title: Anaphase I complete!
recordings.text:
Spindle microtubules shorten and pull homologous chromosomes to opposite poles.

Sister chromatids remain attached at their centromeres. They do not separate in anaphase I.

Each future daughter cell receives one replicated homolog from every pair. This is the reduction division: 2n → n.

recordings.title: Telophase I & cytokinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Tap both chromosome groups to rebuild nuclei.

recordings.title: Telophase I & cytokinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Pinch the cytoplasm into two cells.

recordings.title: Telophase I & cytokinesis complete!
recordings.text:
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into two haploid cells. Each contains one set of replicated chromosomes, not homologous pairs.

In humans, each daughter cell has n = 23 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids. In this model, each has n = 2.

recordings.title: Interkinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Block DNA replication. No second copy!

recordings.title: Interkinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Make proteins for the next division.

recordings.title: Interkinesis complete!
recordings.text:
There is no S phase and no DNA replication between the two meiotic divisions. Copying DNA here earns a penalty and is blocked.

No DNA replication between the two divisions.

recordings.title: Prophase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Tap chromosomes in both cells to re-pack them.

recordings.title: Prophase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Open both nuclear envelopes.

recordings.title: Prophase II complete!
recordings.text:
Chromosomes re-condense in both haploid cells. Spindle apparatuses form and the nuclear envelopes shown in this model break down.

No additional DNA is copied. Each chromosome still consists of two sister chromatids; crossing over can have made those chromatids genetically different.

recordings.title: Metaphase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Choose top or bottom. Connect each sister's kinetochore.

recordings.title: Metaphase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Move chromosomes onto each cell's equator.

recordings.title: Metaphase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Inspect both single-file lineups.

recordings.title: Metaphase II complete!
recordings.text:
Chromosomes align single-file along the equator of each haploid cell.

The kinetochores of sister chromatids connect to spindle fibers from opposite poles. In this scene those poles are at the top and bottom of each cell.

recordings.title: Anaphase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Release the connections at the centromeres.

recordings.title: Anaphase II · Instruction
recordings.text: Now pull sister chromatids apart.

recordings.title: Anaphase II complete!
recordings.text:
Cohesion holding sister chromatids together at their centromeres is released. The DNA at the centromere is not cut out.

Spindle microtubules shorten and separate sister chromatids toward opposite poles of each cell.

Each separated chromatid is now an individual, unreplicated chromosome. Both cells divide their chromosome copies.

recordings.title: Telophase II & cytokinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Tap all four groups to rebuild nuclear envelopes.

recordings.title: Telophase II & cytokinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Unpack chromosomes into chromatin.

recordings.title: Telophase II & cytokinesis · Instruction
recordings.text: Divide both cells. Four haploid products!

recordings.title: Telophase II & cytokinesis complete!
recordings.text:
Four nuclear envelopes form around the isolated chromosome sets. Chromosomes de-condense into extended chromatin.

Cytokinesis divides both cells, producing four genetically nonidentical haploid products in this model.

Each illustrated product has n = 2; human gametes have n = 23. The equal divisions here model gamete formation generally; the oogenesis mode shows unequal cytoplasmic packaging.

recordings.title: Meiosis complete · Instruction
recordings.text:
Four distinct chromosome combinations. Nicely divided.

One diploid precursor has undergone two divisions to form four haploid products. DNA was copied once, before meiosis I. Crossing over and independent assortment create genetic diversity. In this model, the four displayed allele combinations are distinct.
